entries.subject: Challener et al. (2024) JWST NIRSpec white-light eclipse map
entries.finding: The deposited white-light brightness-temperature map (48 x 96 cells, 709.8 to 1975.7 K, hottest cell at +5.625, -13.125 degrees) is the NIRSpec lens (id temperature), shown as deposited. Turned by this package's orbit and synchronous rotation it fits the deposited white-light light curve at reduced chi-squared 2.120 over 4202 samples outside transit; the east-west mirror fits at 16.34 and a uniform planet at 92.75.

entries.subject: Hammond et al. (2024) JWST MIRI/LRS eclipse map
entries.finding: A second-degree spherical-harmonic dayside map from the MIRI phase curve of the Transiting Exoplanet ERS program 1366. The arXiv HTML names no data deposit or repository for the map, so there is no grid to cast. Its longitudinal offset, 7.5 +/- 0.5 degrees east (eigenmapping; 7.75 +/- 0.36 with starry), differs from this package's MIRI lens (6.2 degrees, with light time and the transit time measured in the curve) because the light curve admits two systematics solutions: a fast ramp (0.10 d) with a steep trend and a slow ramp (0.27 d) with a gentle trend. Their Table 1 (ramp 3.7 +/- 0.3 per day and 1319 +/- 66 ppm, trend -240 +/- 60 ppm/day) is the slow solution. On the curve they mapped (Bell et al.'s Eureka! v1 white light, pinned in this package), this repository's fit with their time constant returns ramp 1275 ppm, trend -279 ppm/day, position 0.0120, width -0.0423 and offset 7.45 degrees; the fast ramp gives 5.45 degrees and trend -926 ppm/day, and fits better by chi-squared 14.2 (about 9.5 after their 1.2225 error scaling). This project's reduction shows the same pair, 6.1 and 7.95 degrees. Timing is not the cause: their t0 with Bell et al.'s fitted period (0.81347406 d; the paper prints 0.813474) and starry's barycentric light delay (7.4 s) places the transit 20.6 s before the package ephemeris, where both curves show it (20.5 and 19.5 s). Why their fit chose the slow ramp is not recoverable from the paper; every degree 2 and 3 eigencurve model and a Gaussian stand-in for their pixel prior still prefer the fast ramp here.
entries.revisitWhen: The map grid is deposited as data, or Hammond et al.'s fitting code or priors are published.

entries.subject: Bell et al. (2024) MIRI phase-curve products and models
entries.finding: Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.10525170 (CC BY 4.0, 11.5 MB) holds reduction configurations, light curves, planetary spectra, general circulation model outputs and retrieval posteriors. No two-dimensional observed map; the circulation models are simulations, not observations. A trial fit of the deposited Eureka! v1 white-light curve (5-10.5 micrometres, first 780 integrations and the transit dropped) with this repository's eigencurve fit and the same systematics terms (linear trend, exponential ramp, spatial position and width) prefers degree 2 with 6 eigencurves by BIC. It puts the meridionally averaged hotspot 5.0 degrees east (4.5 to 5.25), against Hammond et al. (2024)'s 7.5 +/- 0.5; changing the systematics model moves it between 3.1 and 5.3. The difference is not resolved, and the trial is not a published map. This repository's raw reduction of the same 30 MIRI segments (tools/objects/jwst/reduce-tso.mts, their settings in Eureka! 1.4) reproduces the deposited white light curve at correlation 0.990 over 9,194 integrations, 172 ppm apart once a 2,221 ppm per day drift is removed, with lower scatter (342 against 373 ppm). The MIRI lenses now come from this project's own reduction of the raw exposures with Bell et al.'s settings (see raw-miri-reduction-lenses); the deposited curve remains the comparison for that reduction.
entries.revisitWhen: A longitude-latitude map fitted to these light curves is published as data.

entries.subject: Single-detector NRS1 and NRS2 maps in the same deposit
entries.finding: The deposit also holds 24 x 48 maps from each NIRSpec detector (2.87-3.72 and 3.82-5.18 microns). The white-light map uses both, has the finer grid and is the one the paper's main results describe; the detector maps agree with it at the 1-sigma level in hotspot position. Their temperature maps are single-wavelength conversions against a blackbody star (see deposit-temperature-conversion).
entries.revisitWhen: A NIRSpec wavelength comparison is wanted as more than a note; see miri-wavelength-slices for why MIRI slices were not kept.

entries.subject: Hotspot latitude under the authors' mapping code
entries.finding: ThERESA at commit 74a8fec on the deposited white-light light curve, transit excluded, 200,000 MCMC samples: degree 3 with 6 eigencurves gives +7.0 and -12.1 degrees (map correlated 0.967 with the deposit). The public code leaves the map's rotation axis in the plane of the sky, 7.8 degrees off the orbit normal (measured in starry); with the axis corrected the same model gives -4.1 degrees (16-84 percent -5.2 to -3.2) at nearly equal chi-squared, and degree 4 with 12 eigencurves gives -16.3 degrees. Longitude (6.9 to 7.2 east) and a southward sign hold in every run; the latitude does not. This repository's own eigencurve fit, which shares no code with starry and spins the planet about the orbit normal, gives the corrected-axis answer independently: chi-squared 8,809.6, hotspot -2.3 and +7.1 degrees, posterior -2.9 (-4.0 to -1.6) and +7.3 (6.9 to 7.5).
entries.revisitWhen: The authors' 2024 code or a map fitted with the rotation axis on the orbit normal is published, or new eclipse data constrain the latitude.

entries.subject: Which side of the star the planet crosses
entries.finding: Photometry cannot tell whether the planet crosses north or south of the stellar centre. Challener et al. assume one side (footnote 1), which fixes the map's north; the package's orbit follows the same construction.
entries.revisitWhen: A measurement that orients the orbit on the sky, such as the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect combined with a stellar inclination, or astrometry.

entries.subject: Position angle of the orbit's ascending node
entries.finding: Transits measure the inclination but not where the orbit's node lies on the sky; the hosted orbit sets it at position angle 0 as a display convention. It does not change the map, the rotation or the light-curve check, only the orbit's orientation among the stars.
entries.revisitWhen: A published sky orientation of the orbit.

entries.subject: Tidal locking of WASP-43b
entries.finding: The rotation record assumes synchronous rotation with the pole on the orbit normal, as both mapping papers assume. It is expected for a 0.81-day orbit but not measured; the light-curve fit is consistent with it.
entries.revisitWhen: A measured rotation rate or obliquity for WASP-43b.

entries.subject: Orbital phase at the scene epoch against independent ephemerides
entries.finding: Propagating the Table 1 transit time and period to 2026-09-03 puts mid-transit 21 s from the Kokori et al. (2023) ephemeris and 39 s from Ivshina & Winn (2022), both from the NASA Exoplanet Archive: 0.1 and 0.2 degrees of orbital phase.

entries.subject: How the deposited NIRSpec temperature maps were converted from flux
entries.finding: The paper converts flux to brightness temperature with a PHOENIX stellar spectrum (4500 K, log g 4.5). In the deposit, the NRS1 and NRS2 maps follow a single-wavelength conversion (3.1551 and 4.466 micrometres) against a 4520 K blackbody star scaled by 1.036 and 1.035: log(B(lambda, T)/flux) varies across cells by 2.7e-7 and 1.4e-6. A model spectrum would not give one scale at both wavelengths: BT-Settl 4500 K sits 8% above that blackbody at 3.16 micrometres and 14% below at 4.47. The white-light map fits no single wavelength (best spread 1.2e-2) and no flat band with a blackbody star (3.2% spread); its conversion is not reproduced. Converted with this package's G395H band and BT-Settl, its flux map is 80 K cooler on the dayside (within 60 degrees) than its temperatures.
entries.revisitWhen: The conversion code or stellar spectrum behind the deposited maps is published.

entries.subject: NIRSpec refit as a lens: this project's fit of the deposited white-light curve
entries.finding: This project's fit of Challener et al.'s white-light curve (degree 3, 6 eigencurves, spin axis on the orbit normal, light time and the measured transit) gave chi-squared 8813.9 over 4202 samples, hot spot -2.34, +7.16 degrees, dayside 1580 K and nightside 875 K. It was a lens from 2026-09-17 and was removed the same day: it reads the same data as the NIRSpec lens, and its differences (spin axis, stellar spectrum, timing) are analysis choices recorded in the README and in theresa-rerun-hotspot-latitude rather than a new measurement. The fit stays checked by eigenmap-fit.test.mts.
entries.revisitWhen: A published NIRSpec map made with the spin axis on the orbit normal, or a decision to show analysis variants as lenses.

entries.subject: MIRI lens from this project's reduction of the raw program 1366 exposures
entries.finding: The 30 raw MIRI/SLITLESSPRISM segments of JWST program 1366 (1-2 December 2022), reduced by tools/objects/jwst/reduce-tso.mts with Bell et al. (2024)'s settings, give the pinned light curves; the tool's white-light export is byte-identical to the pinned file (sha256 a116e36f), and bell-2024-miri-products records its agreement with the deposited curve. Fitted at preparation time with BIC model choice: 5-10.5 micrometres degree 2 with 6 eigencurves, ramp 0.105 d, transit 19.5 s before the package ephemeris, dayside 1527 K and nightside 840 K against Bell et al.'s 1524 +/- 35 and 863 +/- 23 K (5-12 micrometres); longitudinal offset 6.2 degrees east (see hammond-2024-miri-eclipse-map: the difference from Hammond et al.'s 7.5 is their slow-ramp systematics solution). Band weights are the star's own median extracted counts per detector column. The first release (commit 188586d727a9d34acc136b05e53cc027228a755b) stopped the ramp time constant at its 0.08 d grid value and reported the hottest point, 5.3 degrees, as the comparison with Hammond et al. From commit 64baadf1b720ba1e8cb0e941b26b20fb5730a5c5 every fit models light time across the orbit (15 s at eclipse) and takes the transit time from its own light curve.

entries.subject: MIRI wavelength slices (5-6.5, 6.5-8.5, 8.5-10.5 micrometres) as lenses
entries.finding: Three maps fitted to Stage 4 light curves of the same MIRI observation in wide wavelength bins were lenses from 2026-09-17 and were removed the same day. BIC chose degree 2 with 4 eigencurves in each; dayside 1539, 1493 and 1565 K, nightside 835, 837 and 914 K, offsets 3.55, 7.8 and 8.6 degrees east. On a 700-2000 K display these differences are not visible, the offset spread is within what the ramp choice alone moves (about 2 degrees), and at 4 eigencurves every slice put the hottest latitude near +10 degrees, a property of the basis. Wavelength dependence is better described by Bell et al. (2024)'s published dayside and nightside spectra than by near-identical maps.
entries.revisitWhen: A published wavelength-resolved map, or slices that differ by more than the analysis uncertainty.

entries.subject: Distant marker for WASP-43b
entries.finding: The marker is the Challener et al. (2024) NIRSpec brightness-temperature map seen from the host star (substellar point centred, north up, east right) in the lens palette; it replaced the scaffold's flat disc in the palette colour of the dayside mean. It is one fixed image, so it shows the dayside at every orbital phase.
